analysis.one_liner: Bars agencies from issuing any new regulation until they repeal two existing ones.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped any federal agency from issuing a new rule that imposes costs or duties on businesses, individuals, or state and local governments unless the agency first repealed two existing rules of that kind. For major rules — those with $100 million or more in annual economic impact — the new rule's cost would also have to be no greater than the cost of the rules repealed, with the White House budget office certifying that math. Because regulations generally protect someone (workers, consumers, patients, the environment) while costing a regulated party, this formula would have put a hard cap on the total amount of federal regulation: no new protection without two old ones coming off the books first.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and other regulated parties that bear the cost of federal rules. A two-for-one repeal requirement, with a cost ceiling for major rules, would have made the stock of costly regulation permanently shrink or stay flat, limiting new compliance burdens. Larger firms have the biggest compliance budgets and would have gained the most relief; industry groups have historically backed this kind of pay-as-you-go rulemaking.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits an agency from issuing a rule that imposes a cost or responsibility on a nongovernmental person or a state or local government unless the agency has repealed two or more such rules, related to the new rule to the extent practicable.

For major rules (generally those with $100 million or more in annual economic effect), the agency must also have repealed two related rules, and the cost of the new major rule must be less than or equal to the cost of the rules repealed, certified by the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs at OMB.
Any rule repealed under the bill must be published in the Federal Register, giving the public a record of what was removed.

analysis.who_pays: The people who rely on what federal regulations deliver — workplace safety rules, clean air and water standards, consumer financial protections, food and drug safety, and similar protections — would have faced a system in which old protections must be eliminated before new ones can be created. The bill counts rules and compares costs but takes no account of the benefits of the rule repealed or the rule issued, so a life-saving new safeguard could only move forward if two costly older protections were scrapped. State and local governments, which are covered by the bill, would also bear the effects of rules repealed or blocked.

drawbacks.text: The bill's formula counts rules and dollars but not benefits: an agency could repeal two significant protections to issue one new rule, as long as the repealed rules' costs were high enough, with no requirement that what was lost mattered less than what was gained.

The requirement applies to any new rule imposing costs on nongovernmental persons or state and local governments, and does not apply to agencies' internal policies or to rule revisions that reduce burdens — meaning the constraint lands squarely on rules that bind outside parties.

Rules are not interchangeable: repealing, say, a paperwork rule does not offset eliminating a safety standard, yet the bill treats them as fungible cost units, which is the core of the objection to one-in-two-out schemes generally.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For businesses, the benefit is straightforward: a hard limit on new regulatory burdens and a mechanism that forces agencies to retire old rules. The cost falls on the diffuse public side of the ledger — the protections regulation provides — and the bill's own design makes that cost likely, because it requires repeals regardless of whether the repealed rules' benefits exceeded their costs. As drafted, it is a fairly blunt instrument: a carefully-tailored version might have encouraged pruning of obsolete rules, but this version would have applied to every new cost-imposing rule, including narrow ones.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and later to a subcommittee, no committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael McCaul introduced the One In, Two Out Act in the House on August 2, 2013.
On the day of introduction, the Speaker referred it to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and, in addition, to the Committee on the Judiciary.
On September 13, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law, and no further action appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress.
The bill never received a markup, a committee vote, or a floor vote in either chamber, and died at the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.
The bill drew 25 cosponsors, all Republicans, but no Senate companion action is in the record and no vote was ever taken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal regulatory protections are better off, since nothing required agencies to repeal two existing rules before issuing a new one. Businesses hoping for a cap on new regulation gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on federal protections

for.name: Rep. Michael McCaul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the One In, Two Out Act on August 2, 2013.

for.name: 25 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Reps. Williams, Thornberry, Jenkins, Conaway, Rice of South Carolina, Pearce, Neugebauer, and Cook.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Darrell Issa (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill on August 2, 2013 and never reported it out or scheduled a markup.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Secondary committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Bob Goodlatte (R)
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill on August 2, 2013 and never took it up; its Regulatory Reform subcommittee received a further referral on September 13, 2013 with no resulting action.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 cosponsors were Republicans, and no votes were ever taken, so no division on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Regulated businesses (manufacturing, energy, finance, and others bearing federal compliance costs)
industries.note: The bill would have capped the growth of costly regulation by requiring two repeals for every new rule and cost-neutrality for major rules. The gain to these industries comes directly out of the protections regulation provides to workers, consumers, and the public.

The bill covers rules that impose costs or responsibilities on states, localities, and tribes, so it could relieve them of mandates — but it equally blocks any new rule that would benefit them, and requires them to give up rules to make way for new ones.

industries.industry: Federal agencies and the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs
industries.note: Agencies would have lost the ability to issue new cost-imposing rules freely, and OIRA would have gained a certification role over major-rule cost comparisons.
